extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, administrators, investigators, and legal counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for structuring and operating Title IX grievance procedures, including required timeframes, privacy protections, handling of law-enforcement overlap, evidence disclosure/redaction, training, and related due-process safeguards. Targeted to institutions implementing the final Title IX regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prompt timeframes for grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must set, and abide by, reasonably prompt timeframes for the major stages of their grievance procedures; timeframes must be reasonable and for good cause, and recipients may not have indefinite grievance procedures or hide the nature of required timeframes or reasons for an extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department declines to set a specific minimum or maximum timeframe or require business/calendar days; recipients have flexibility to designate appropriate timeframes based on their environment. Parties who believe a recipient failed to comply with reasonably prompt timeframes may file a complaint with OCR. The Department notes the availability of supportive measures during pendency and emergency removal under §106.44(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case extensions for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may provide reasonable extension[s] of timeframes on a case-by-case basis for good cause, and (for postsecondary institutions subject to the Clery Act) must give written notice to the parties that includes the reason for the delay (see §106.46(e)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department removed exhaustive examples of good cause to avoid implying mandatory extensions. Illustrative good-cause examples (not exclusive) include absence of a party, advisor, or witness; recipients should consider alternatives (e.g., videoconference, choosing an available advisor) before extending. Recipients must not delay provision of supportive measures because of an extension. Decisionmakers may not draw an inference based solely on a party's or witness's refusal to answer (see §106.46(f)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility on the 60‑day timeframe (no fixed statutory timeframe)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to reinstate a single required timeframe (such as 60 days) and instead leaves it to recipients to determine reasonable timelines; recipients that find 60 days reasonable may adopt it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department references prior rulemaking comments both for complainants (that procedures often take too long) and recipients (that fair procedures can take more than 60 days). Recipients should balance promptness with fairness and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statute of limitations for filing sex-discrimination complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to adopt a statute of limitations for filing a Title IX sex-discrimination complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing a filing deadline would be unfair to complainants who may delay reporting for many reasons and would not further Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of major stages of a grievance procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of major stages include evaluation, investigation, determination, and appeal; the Department revised the evaluation-stage wording to 'the recipient's decision whether to dismiss or investigate a complaint of sex discrimination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may identify additional stages and provide timeframes for those stages if helpful for parties' understanding. The evaluation stage is a major stage and parties should be informed of its timeframe for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling overlap with law-enforcement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to delay Title IX grievance procedures for concurrent law-enforcement proceedings, nor is such a delay absolutely prohibited; a concurrent law-enforcement proceeding may sometimes constitute good cause for an extension, on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are encouraged to avoid unnecessary delays; supportive measures must continue regardless of law-enforcement involvement. Recipients remain obligated to operate programs free from sex discrimination and may take actions permitted by the regulations during pendency of law-enforcement proceedings. Recipients must also heed §106.44(j) when disclosing information to law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections during the pendency of grievance procedures (§106.45(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5) requires a recipient to take reasonable steps to protect the parties' and witnesses' privacy during the pendency of grievance procedures, provided these steps do not restrict the parties' ability to: obtain and present evidence, consult with family members, confidential resources, or advisors, or otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What constitutes 'reasonable steps' varies with circumstances. Any steps that infringe constitutional rights or otherwise undermine due process are inherently unreasonable and do not qualify. The Department modified phrasing to 'otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.' The provision is not synonymous with a 'confidential employee' concept; a 'confidential resource' need not be an employee but must have confidential status under law or profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using privacy measures to restrict evidence-gathering or participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not take reasonable steps to protect privacy if those steps restrict the parties' ability to gather evidence, consult certain individuals, or prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures — §106.45(b)(5) prohibits such restrictive uses of privacy protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other regulatory provisions supplement these protections (e.g., §106.45(f)(2) on opportunity to present witnesses and evidence, §106.46(e)(2) on advisors in certain postsecondary cases, and §106.6(g) on parental/guardian participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to prevent and address unauthorized disclosures of grievance-only materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 106.45(f)(4)(iii) and 106.46(e)(6)(iii) require recipients to prevent and address parties' unauthorized disclosure of material obtained solely through the grievance procedures, and any steps to do so must be reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is overlap among §§106.45(b)(5), 106.45(f)(4)(iii), and 106.46(e)(6)(iii); certain steps may further multiple provisions. Recipients must consider the different aims (general privacy protection vs preventing disclosure of materials obtained only via grievance procedures) when designing safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on redaction of evidence and information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may redact information that is not relevant to the allegations; however, recipients must not redact information or evidence that is relevant to the allegations of sex discrimination and not otherwise impermissible, because such redaction infringes on parties' rights to access relevant evidence and on due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must redact or refrain from disclosing information impermissible under §106.45(b)(7) (e.g., privileged information, records made by treatment providers, evidence about sexual interests/prior sexual conduct except narrow exceptions). The Department explains constitutional and GEPA overrides justify disclosure of otherwise FERPA-protected records when necessary for due process; where the constitutional override does not apply, the GEPA override may require compliance with Title IX rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of nondisclosure/confidentiality agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations neither require nor prohibit nondisclosure agreements (NDAs); NDAs fall within a recipient's discretion to determine reasonable steps to protect privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient requires an NDA, it must still comply with all applicable Title IX requirements including §106.45(b)(5). Recipients may not condition the offer/coordination of supportive measures or initiation of grievance procedures on signing an NDA. Overly broad NDAs may not satisfy the reasonableness requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections after conclusion of grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5) does not apply after the conclusion of the grievance procedures; however, Title IX's prohibitions on harassment and retaliation, §106.44(j) limitations on disclosure of personally identifiable information obtained while carrying out Title IX obligations, and other privacy laws (e.g., FERPA) continue to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to extend §106.45(b)(5) beyond the conclusion because post-conclusion disclosure presents less threat to fairness and integrity of a specific investigation/outcome. §106.44(j) and other laws provide continued privacy constraints with specified exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'confidential resource' and 'advisor'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Confidential resource' is not synonymous with 'confidential employee'; it need not be an employee but must have confidential status under federal, state, or local law or by virtue of profession (e.g., mental health counselor or community rape crisis counselor typically qualify). 'Advisor' refers to any individual acting as advisor to the party for purposes of the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to broaden the list of persons with whom parties may consult beyond family members, confidential resources, or advisors, but recipients may allow consultations with additional individuals at their discretion. Other provisions (e.g., §106.6(g), §106.46(e)(2)-(3)) may limit when/how a party communicates with these individuals in specific proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with retaliation and witness intimidation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's right to speak to witnesses is subject to the requirement in §106.71 that a recipient prohibit retaliation, defined as 'intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination' intended to interfere with rights or because someone participated in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must comply with both privacy protections and retaliation prohibitions. §106.71 may bar conduct that chills witness participation; recipients should enforce anti-retaliation safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' authority and discretion to determine reasonable privacy steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Because privacy measures are fact-specific, the Department declines to provide detailed privacy guidelines (including sanctioning employees); recipients are best positioned to determine reasonable steps based on circumstances, nature of allegations, and stage of the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must operate within the parameters of §106.45(b)(5) and related provisions; the Department revised §106.44(j) to prohibit certain disclosures of personally identifiable information. Recipients must ensure their chosen steps do not infringe constitutional/due-process rights or other regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required training for employees and role-holders
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.8(d)(2)(ii) requires recipients to ensure that employees and individuals who have any role in implementing Title IX regulations receive training on the recipient's grievance procedures to the extent related to their responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This training requirement inherently includes privacy-related training necessary to comply with §§106.45(b)(5), 106.45(f)(4)(iii), and 106.46(e)(6)(iii). Recipients may also train on other privacy laws (FERPA, HIPAA) or methods to protect sensitive data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on access/use of medical/therapy records without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.45(b)(7)(ii), a party's or witness's records made or maintained by a physician, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional related to treatment must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used as part of the grievance procedures unless the party/witness gives voluntary, written consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related discussion of §§106.45(b)(6) and (7) for narrow exceptions and interplay with evidence disclosure/redaction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of allegations and identities as part of due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.45(c)(1)(ii), parties are entitled to a notice of the allegations that includes the identities of the parties involved in the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes this requirement supports parties' ability to organize a defense and helps balance privacy with due process; recipients may not withhold relevant information that is not impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative sequencing to reduce witness influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations prohibits a recipient from requiring its investigator to speak to witnesses prior to speaking with the parties to minimize the risk that witness statements will be improperly influenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sequencing is noted as a permissible practice to mitigate witness intimidation or improper influence while preserving parties' rights to access evidence and participate.
